objectives: Stay strictly inside the passage — distinguish 'true' from 'supported'
Match Command-of-Evidence choices to the specific claim in the stem
Make only inferences the text logically forces

slides.title: Part 1 — Why Information & Ideas dominates Reading & Writing
slides.body: This is the single highest-leverage verbal domain on the SAT. Treat it as a discipline, not a reading-comprehension hope, and it becomes the most reliable points on the test.

slides.title: What it actually tests — the four question types
slides.body:
Digital-SAT Reading & Writing is single short passages with one question each. Information & Ideas is ~26% of that section and comes in four flavors, all testing one underlying discipline — *staying strictly inside the text*:

1. **Central Ideas** — the main point the whole passage is built to support (not a true detail, the *thesis*).
2. **Command of Evidence (textual)** — which sentence/quotation best supports a given claim or conclusion.
3. **Command of Evidence (quantitative)** — which data point from a graph/table best supports a claim (you read the figure, not prose).
4. **Inferences** — what *must* logically follow from the passage alone (fill the blank with the entailed conclusion).

Every one is graded against the passage, never against world knowledge, plausibility, or what merely sounds smart.

slides.title: The one rule that fixes most mistakes
slides.body:
> **The discipline:** the credited answer is the one the passage *forces*, not the one that is merely true, reasonable, or appealing.

The SAT's signature wrong answer is a statement that is **factually correct but unsupported by *this* text**. Your brain wants to reward truth and fluency; the test punishes exactly that reflex. Internal habit on every choice: *"Which specific sentence here makes this necessarily true?"* If you cannot put your finger on it, the choice is wrong — no matter how good it sounds. This single move is worth more raw points than any vocabulary study.

slides.title: Part 2 — Strategy a top scorer uses
Read the question stem first — and why it works
slides.body: On Information & Ideas, read the *question* before the choices and (often) before re-reading the passage. The stem names the job precisely — "main idea", "best supports the claim that X", "most strongly suggests", "which finding would weaken". Reading the passage *with the job in mind* turns passive comprehension into a targeted hunt: you're searching for one specific thing, not absorbing everything equally. Top scorers are not faster readers; they are more *directed* readers, and the stem is the direction.

slides.title: Evidence questions: the answer must do a *job*, not be *true*
slides.body: A Command-of-Evidence choice is not graded on truth — it is graded on **function**: does it support *the exact claim named in the stem*? A quotation can be the most striking, most true line in the passage and still be wrong because it supports a *different* claim. Procedure: (1) restate the stem's claim in your own words; (2) for each choice ask only "does this make *that* claim more justified?"; (3) reject true-but-off-claim and vivid-but-off-claim choices ruthlessly. Function over truth — write it on your hand.

slides.title: Quantitative evidence: axes before data, claim before choices
slides.body: Graph/table items add a misread layer. Disciplined order: (1) read **axis labels and units** *before* looking at any value; (2) restate the stem's claim; (3) find the single data feature that makes *that* claim true (a comparison, a trend direction, a threshold). The three wrong-answer factories here: misreading an axis/unit, citing a true-but-irrelevant value, and overstating a trend the data only weakly shows. The data is not hard; the *reading* of it is the test.

slides.title: Part 3 — Worked examples, end to end
Worked example 1 — the passage + stem
slides.body:
*Passage (paraphrased):* "Researchers found urban crows made 30% fewer tool-making attempts after observing a skilled crow, while a control group's attempt rate was unchanged. The authors conclude social observation accelerates skill acquisition in corvids."

*Stem:* Which finding, if true, would most directly **support** the authors' conclusion?

First restate the claim: *observation makes skill come faster*. The key word is **accelerates** — a claim about *rate*.

slides.title: Worked example 1 — walking every choice
slides.body:
- *"Crows in both groups eventually reached the same skill level."* — true-sounding, but says nothing about *speed via observation*; it's about endpoint, not rate. **Off-claim trap.**
- *"The observing group reached proficiency in half the time of the control group."* — directly evidences *accelerated* acquisition *attributable to observation*. **Credited.**
- *"Urban crows are more intelligent than rural crows."* — outside-knowledge flavor, unsupported, irrelevant to the claim. **Trap.**

Every wrong choice is grammatical and plausible; only one does the *job the stem asked for*. That is the entire game.

question.question: A claim states: "social observation *accelerates* skill learning." Which evidence type best supports the word *accelerates*?
options: A comparison of how *fast* each group learned
Proof that both groups were equally motivated
A statement that crows are skilled tool users
The total number of crows studied
question.explanation: "Accelerates" is about *rate*. Only a speed/time comparison between groups evidences a rate claim; the others are off-claim even if true.

slides.title: Worked example 2 — an inference under hedges
slides.body:
*Passage:* "The study's sample was small and drawn from a single clinic; the authors note results may not generalize." *Stem:* The passage most strongly implies that…

The credited inference must **survive the passage's own caveats**. A sweeping choice ("the treatment works for the general population") contradicts the explicit hedge and is wrong *because the text limited itself*. The right answer is correspondingly cautious ("more study is needed before broad claims"). Inference = entailment given *everything* the passage says, **including its limitations**. Overreach is the designed trap.

slides.title: The four trap families to name on sight
slides.body:
Wrong answers on Information & Ideas are manufactured, not random. Learn the factory:

1. **True-but-unsupported** — correct in the world, no sentence here forces it.
2. **Off-claim** — supports a *different* claim than the stem names (the favorite on evidence items).
3. **Overreach** — ignores a hedge/limitation the passage stated.
4. **Half-right** — one clause matches, another contradicts the text (the most dangerous; you must read the *whole* choice).

Naming the trap as you eliminate is faster and more reliable than re-reading the passage four times.

question.question: Diagnose the mistake.
question.scenario: A student answers an evidence question by choosing the quotation that is the most memorable, dramatic sentence in the passage. It's a real line from the text — but they get the question wrong.

rubricCriteria.description: identifies that 'is in the passage / is striking' is not the criterion
states the choice must support the SPECIFIC claim in the stem
recommends matching the quotation's function to the claim, not its vividness

question.explanation: Command-of-Evidence is judged by *function*, not presence or drama. A real, vivid line that supports a different claim is the SAT's signature trap.

hints: The text explicitly limits how far you can conclude.
Which choice could the author still endorse given those limits?
slides.workedSolution: Inference = what *must* follow given everything the passage says, including its caveats. When a passage hedges, the credited answer is correspondingly cautious; overstated choices contradict the hedge and are wrong.

question.question: A passage describes a study's *limitations*. The stem asks for the choice the passage "most strongly implies." Best approach?
options: Pick the modest claim the limitations still allow — avoid choices that overstate the result
Use outside knowledge about the topic
question.explanation: Inference answers must survive the passage's own hedges. If the text flags limitations, the supported inference is cautious; sweeping choices are traps.

question.question: "Most reasonable inference" on the SAT means the choice that is:
options: Logically forced by statements in the passage
Consistent with what you already know
question.explanation: Inference questions are deductive within the passage. 'Reasonable' = entailed by the text, not plausible-in-general.

question.prompt: Explain to a friend the difference between an answer that is *true* and an answer that is *supported by the passage* — and why the SAT loves the gap between them.

rubricCriteria.description: 'true' = correct in the world; 'supported' = the text makes it necessarily so
the SAT's classic trap is true-but-unsupported
correct strategy: point to the exact line that forces the answer

question.question: In 2–3 sentences, give your own rule for attacking any Command-of-Evidence question.

rubricCriteria.description: reads the specific claim in the stem first
selects the choice whose function is to support THAT claim
rejects choices that are true/vivid but off-claim

slides.title: How it scores & what's next
slides.body: Information & Ideas is ~26–28% of Reading & Writing — the highest-leverage verbal domain, and the most *trainable* because the discipline (stay in the text; match evidence to the exact claim; respect hedges) is mechanical once internalized. The same function-over-content reading directly powers the next domain, **Craft & Structure**, where the question shifts from *what* a text says to *how and why* it says it.
